newsitem.title: USA: Albright's honeymoon may not last long.
newsitem.headline: Albright's honeymoon may not last long.

text.p: Madeleine Albright's vaunted diplomatic and political skills were on full display last week as she effortlessly aced her confirmation hearing en route to Senate approval as America's first female secretary of state.

But the honeymoon is unlikely to last long. There are bound to be tensions with the Republican-led Congress, and others, as she helps lead U.S. foreign policy into the next century -- encouraging greater U.S. international activism, building Europe's new security framework, managing ties with China and integrating Russia into the West, among other challenges.

The largely-male 18-member Senate Foreign Relations Committee, which must endorse her appointment by President Bill Clinton ahead of full Senate approval, was almost embarrassingly lavish in its praise of the nominee.

Even Republican Jesse Helms, the panel's chairman, left his tendency toward irascibility at the hearing room door. Showing his courtly side, he called it a "joy" to work with Albright in her role since 1993 as United Nations ambassador.

It was a contrast to the hearing faced four years ago by the current secretary of state, Warren Christopher. Then the questioning had more of an edge and Helms himself acknowledged "reservations" about that appointment.

The smooth committee ritual was not left to chance. As is the custom, Albright met with Helms and other senators before the hearing so they could explore difficult issues in private. She also spent hours in closed-door sessions with aides, practicing answers she would give the committee in public.
At the hearing, many Albright answers were deliberately vague to avoid controversy that could derail the nomination or lock her into early commitments she wasn't prepared to make.
"She has to walk a fine line between having been part of the administration for the last four years but also wanting to approach the new job with a new imprint," one official said.

A former congressional aide and adviser to Democratic presidential candidates, she scored big points by repeatedly promising to work with Congress, to be pragmatic and to "tell it like it is, here and when I go abroad."
The senators, perhaps encouraged by what they heard in private, did not aggressively try to pin her down, although their queries became more probing as the hearing ran on.

Still, while she played a major role in helping Clinton make foreign policy in his first term, Albright seemed largely to escape being held responsible for policies the senators found fault with, like the U.S. invasion of Haiti.

Even with new Republican-Democrat commitments to bipartisanship in foreign policy, however, Albright could soon encounter rougher waters. Pledges by the newly-installed Congress to cooperate on domestic issues already are fraying.

As the first woman, and a passionate Democrat who immigrated to the United States from Czechoslovakia after fleeing Nazism and communism in Europe, Albright has already brought new energy to the secretary of state's job.
Her plan to persuade Congress and the American people of the need for a new U.S. engagement in the world could be quite a challenge in a country where isolationism is on the rise.

Although many agree with NATO's plans to expand into former communist states in eastern Europe, the debate is likely to become more fractured when Congress formally is asked to extend U.S. and NATO security guarantees to new members.

While viewed by advocates as sincerely committed to human rights, Albright was ambiguous about integrating those concerns in China policy. She vowed to speak out forcefully on abuses and threatened to propose this year that the U.N. Human Rights Commission adopt a resolution faulting Beijing's rights policy.

But she stressed her main aim, like Christopher's, would be to integrate, not isolate, Beijing, into the world community. She also emphasized promoting U.S. economic growth, raising doubts about whether human rights would lose out to trade priorities as often occurred in Christopher's tenure.

Albright pushed Congress to reverse severe cuts in foreign affairs funding and pay $1 billion in back U.N. dues. But she has to prove first that U.N. reforms are credible and must grapple with the demand by Helms and others for U.S. foreign affairs agencies to be restructured.
